title: Gold Returned 60% Last Diwali and 13% This One; Analysts Target $5,000 Next
excerpt: Diwali-to-Diwali data show gold beating the Nifty five years running despite a record high and a sharp 2026 correction — and what brokerages expect for Samvat 2083.
body:
• Domestic gold returned 60.21% Diwali-to-Diwali in 2025 (Rs 79,181 to Rs 1,26,854 per 10 grams) but 12.87% in 2026, reaching Rs 1,43,184 by November 5, according to Mirae Asset Sharekhan data reported by The Times of India.
  • Gold beat the Nifty in each of the last five Diwali-to-Diwali years; in the latest year the Nifty fell 5.06% while domestic gold rose 12.87%, even though spot gold in dollars fell 5.81%.
  • The 2026 ride was violent: a record $5,595 an ounce on January 29, then a fall to a one-year low of $3,870 in November after the Fed turned hawkish.
  • For Samvat 2083, Mirae Asset Sharekhan's 12-month target is $5,000 an ounce, and Motilal Oswal advises buying on dips with an accumulation zone near $3,800–3,900 — forecasts, not guarantees, and best acted on in stages rather than in one Dhanteras purchase.

Gold enters this Dhanteras with a two-year record that explains both the queues and the caution. Measured Diwali to Diwali, domestic gold prices rose 60.21% in the year to October 20, 2025 — from Rs 79,181 to Rs 1,26,854 per 10 grams — and then 12.87% in the year to November 5, 2026, reaching Rs 1,43,184, according to Mirae Asset Sharekhan data reported by The Times of India. In dollar terms, spot gold gained 58.80% in the first of those years and fell 5.81% in the second; the rupee price stayed positive partly because the currency moved the other way.

Five straight years ahead of equities

The longer record is why gold keeps its place in family portfolios. Diwali-time prices have climbed from about Rs 30,000 per 10 grams in 2016 to nearly Rs 1.50 lakh in 2026, and gold's Diwali-to-Diwali return has beaten the Nifty in each of the last five years — including 31.90% against the Nifty's 23.97% in 2024 and 20.50% against 10.12% in 2023. In the latest year, the comparison was starker: the Nifty fell 5.06% and the Sensex 8.37% while domestic gold rose 12.87%.

Motilal Oswal's analysis adds a seasonal pattern: over the past decade, gold has generally performed better in the 30 days before Diwali than in the month after it. In 2025, gold rose nearly 20% and silver about 38% in the 30 days leading up to Diwali. Motilal Oswal reads Diwali as a seasonal trigger for demand and positioning rather than a one-day price event, with the scale of returns ultimately set by the global macroeconomic backdrop. For the festival's traditions and legends, see our explainer on why families buy gold on Dhanteras.

A record high, then a sharp reversal

The smaller 2026 return hides an extreme ride. Spot gold hit a record $5,595 an ounce on January 29, 2026 — up nearly 30% year-to-date at that point, on top of a 65% gain in 2025 — driven by expected US rate cuts, de-dollarisation, geopolitical tension, fiscal-deficit worries and a weaker dollar. Then the script flipped. Praveen Singh, head of commodities at Mirae Asset Sharekhan, told TOI the outlook turned with the nomination of Kevin Warsh to succeed Jerome Powell as Fed chair, because markets read Warsh as an advocate of monetary discipline. After the US-Israel attack on Iran on February 28 pushed oil and inflation higher, expectations swung from three rate cuts to three rate hikes; the Fed raised rates in September for the first time in more than three years, and gold fell to $3,870 an ounce in November, its lowest in a year. In India, the fall was cushioned somewhat by the rise in excise duty to 15%, TOI reported. A separate market analysis put the MCX spot fall at 19.2%, from Rs 1,75,231 per 10 grams on January 29 to Rs 1,41,498 on October 29.

"Gold's longer-term structural drivers remain supportive. Fiscal deficits across major economies remain elevated, sovereign debt continues to rise, and central banks are accumulating gold as they diversify their reserves."

— Praveen Singh, Head of Commodities, Mirae Asset Sharekhan, to TOI

The outlook for Samvat 2083

Analysts quoted by TOI remain constructive for the new Samvat, with numbers attached. Mirae Asset Sharekhan's 12-month target is $5,000 an ounce — about 29% above the November low of $3,870 — and Singh said a move toward $6,000 over a longer horizon cannot be ruled out if fiscal, geopolitical and monetary risks intensify, pointing to US public debt above $40 trillion and annual interest payments above $1 trillion. Motilal Oswal maintains a buy-on-dips stance: an accumulation zone near $3,800–3,900, short-term targets of $4,200 and medium-term targets of $4,500–4,700; in rupee terms, assuming USD-INR at 96, it calls Rs 1,35,000 a good accumulation zone, with Rs 1,48,000 as a short-term target and Rs 1,60,000–1,68,000 over the medium term.

Other houses counsel patience rather than a single festive purchase. World Gold Council data cited in a TradingView market analysis showed global gold demand rose about 2% in the first half of 2026 to 2,522 tonnes, a record $380 billion in value, and Motilal Oswal's Manav Modi advised accumulating in stages on dips. InCred Money's Vijay Kuppa put the reader's choice plainly in the same analysis: gold is fairly priced if US rates stop rising and expensive if they do not — which is why the experts' shared advice for Samvat 2083 is staggered buying, treating gold as a diversifier rather than a trade. These are analysts' forecasts and views, not guarantees; readers should weigh them against their own plans and, for large purchases, a SEBI-registered adviser.
